name: Sara Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for the Meyer brothers at Brookside, which is four hundred outdoor sows and about a hundred and fifty hectares of wheat and barley that mostly goes back into the pig feed. I look after the farrowing paddocks, that's where the sows have their piglets in little huts, so my day is checking every hut, counting litters, moving straw, and pulling out the odd piglet that's got itself stuck. At harvest I drive the grain trailer. I've been there seven years, since I finished my agriculture certificate.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the piglets, I'm not ashamed to say it, and I like that the Meyers trust me with the farrowing. What wears me out is the mud in winter and the pay, which is the same as the lads who just drive. I'm engaged to Daniel, he's a joiner, and the wedding's next August at our church, so every spare penny is going into that. We've got maybe two weeks of money that isn't wedding money. I use the AI chat thing now and then, mostly for wedding lists, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Well, that's what my granddad said it would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a fad, mostly, but some of it was handy. I'd probably say at church that people should have spent less time on screens anyway. I'm not one for posting opinions online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means our plans go ahead. Wedding in August, then saving for a house, then children, God willing. If the biggest change is that the chat thing helps me write a seating plan, I'll take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the farrowing and keep saving for the wedding. I'd keep using the chat tool now and then for lists and maybe the sow records. After the wedding, I'd start putting a bit aside every month for a house deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Happy, really. Nothing in the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the biggest risk to those plans in a normal year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Disease, probably. If the pigs got swine fever or something, the Meyers would be in real trouble, and so would I. That's the thing that keeps farmers up, not computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think makes farming hard at the moment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The supermarkets with their prices, and the paperwork from the government. The Meyers spend a day a week on forms. If people left farmers alone to farm, we'd do fine.

S0.say: It was mostly a fad, though some of it was handy. People should have spent less time on screens anyway, she'd say at church.
S0.think: Her plans go ahead: the wedding in August, then a house and children. If AI only helps with a seating plan, that's fine with her.
S0.do: Carries on with the farrowing and saves for the wedding. Keeps using the chat tool now and then for lists and sow records. Starts saving monthly for a house deposit after the wedding.
S0.feel: Calm and happy, with nothing in the way.
S0.quote: If the biggest change is that the chat thing helps me write a seating plan, I'll take it.
S0.fieldNote: Sara's life is organised around next August's wedding and the steps after it. Her real fear is pig disease, not technology. She blames supermarkets and government paperwork, in line with her free-market, traditional views.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Many jobs changing. The farrowing? I don't know, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say every generation has new tools and we get on with it. I'd say families and churches will help people through, like they always have. I'd be sensible about it, not dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the Meyers would get cameras and sensors in the farrowing huts, because they're already looking at them. A camera can count piglets, but it can't climb into a hut at two in the morning and turn a breech piglet round. So I think I'd keep my job, but there'd be fewer of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until the Meyers had the cameras in and working, then learn how they work properly, using the chat tool to help. I'd keep the wedding as planned. I'd maybe hold off on the house deposit for a year, just to keep a bit more cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A worry in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Brookside would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tobias, who's sixty and drives the feed lorry round the paddocks. That's exactly the sort of job a machine would do. He's been there thirty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said families and churches would help people through. Is that enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For most things, yes. Our church helped the Brauns when their barn burned. For a lot of people losing work at once, I don't know. Maybe not.

S1.say: Every generation has new tools and we get on with it. Families and churches will help people through, as they always have.
S1.think: The Meyers would bring cameras and sensors into the farrowing huts, leaving fewer workers. She expects to keep her job because some tasks still need a person at night.
S1.do: Waits until the farm's cameras are in and working, then learns them properly with help from the chat tool. Keeps the wedding plans. Holds off on the house deposit for a year to keep a cushion.
S1.feel: Uneasy, a worry in the background.
S1.quote: A camera can count piglets, but it can't climb into a hut at two in the morning and turn a breech piglet round.
S1.fieldNote: Sara trusts her hands-on skill at night farrowing to keep her job. She leans on church and family as the safety net but admits doubt when many lose work at once. Her steady approach is to learn the cameras once they're proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's the year after the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to pray and pull together, and I'd mean it. I'd also say the government shouldn't let these companies tear through everything with no warning, which isn't what I'd normally say. I'd say it to the Meyers and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Brookside would end up all robots, or be sold to a big company that runs it that way. Daniel's joinery would go too, if robots can do hands-on work. We'd be newlyweds with two weeks of money and two trades a machine does better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Daniel about moving the wedding to something tiny, just family at the church, and keeping the wedding money as savings. I'd cut back on everything else. I'd ask my parents and his whether we could live with one of them for a year if it came to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake. Sad, too, about the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut from the wedding first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hall and the band. The church is free, more or less, and my aunt would do a buffet. I'd keep the dress, I've already paid for the dress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try to learn something new in those two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to, but I'd want to see what works first, and there's no time. I'd probably try to get onto whatever retraining the government offered, even though I don't like relying on them.

S2.say: People need to pray and pull together. The government shouldn't let companies tear through everything without warning, which isn't her usual view.
S2.think: Brookside would be automated or sold, and her fiancé's joinery would go too. They'd be newlyweds with two weeks of money.
S2.do: Shrinks the wedding to a small church service and keeps the wedding money as savings. Cuts back on all other spending. Asks both sets of parents about living with them for a year.
S2.feel: Alarmed and losing sleep, and sad about the wedding.
S2.quote: I'd keep the dress, I've already paid for the dress.
S2.fieldNote: The wedding is the first thing Sara would sacrifice, and she'd keep only the dress she's already paid for. She'd accept government help reluctantly, against her instincts. Faith and family are her first responses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. We'd be married, maybe with a baby on the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to prepare, so let's not panic. I'd say young people should learn trades that will last, and the Meyers should train their workers on the new machines. I'd be calm in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years means we'd have to think hard about children. I'd want to know where our money would come from before we had them. The farrowing job would probably last three or four years, then not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the wedding but smaller, and put the difference into savings. I'd wait a year or two to see which machines the bigger pig farms were buying, then ask the Meyers to send me on a course to run them. We'd probably put off having children by a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Clear worry, but I'd feel I had some hold on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would putting off children feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hard. My mum had me at twenty-three. I'd want to be a mum by thirty. Putting it off because of robots would feel wrong somehow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years buy you, compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our wedding, really. In two years it's a sandwich in the church hall. In five we'd have a proper day and some savings, and time to see what jobs were left.

S3.say: There's time to prepare, so let's not panic. Young people should learn lasting trades and the Meyers should train their workers on the new machines.
S3.think: Her farrowing job would last three or four years. They'd have to think hard about having children until they knew where the money would come from.
S3.do: Keeps the wedding but smaller and saves the difference. Waits a year or two to see which machines bigger pig farms buy, then asks to be trained on them. Puts off children by a couple of years.
S3.feel: Anxious, with some sense of control.
S3.quote: In two years it's a sandwich in the church hall.
S3.fieldNote: For Sara, the extra time protects her wedding but threatens her timeline for children. Delaying children feels wrong to her, tied to her mother's example. Her steady approach shows in waiting to see which machines win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. Hopefully with two little ones by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty to adjust, if families and communities pull together. I'd want the farms to train their own people, apprenticeships rather than handouts. I'd say it in church and to the Meyers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think ten years is long enough for me to move into running the machines at Brookside, or to do something else with animals. The robots can have the mud, I'll keep the night shifts with the sows. I'd want a part that needs a person, and I think farrowing has a bit of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go ahead with the wedding as planned and start saving for a house after. In three or four years, once the Meyers had chosen their systems, I'd learn to run them. We'd have children when we'd planned, maybe starting in a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More hopeful than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robots can have the mud. What part would you hold onto?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bit where a sow's in trouble and you have to decide quickly. I've lost piglets and saved piglets, and you learn it by doing it. I'd want to be the one the robot calls when it doesn't know what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about where you live or your plans with Daniel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Daniel's family have been in the village for generations, and so has the church. We'd stay and make it work.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty to adjust if families and communities pull together. Farms should train their own people through apprenticeships, not handouts.
S4.think: Ten years is long enough to move into running the farm's machines or another animal job. She'd hold onto the parts that need a person, like night farrowing.
S4.do: Goes ahead with the wedding as planned and saves for a house after. Learns the farm's new systems in three or four years once they're chosen. Keeps her plans for children.
S4.feel: Uneasy but more hopeful than worried.
S4.quote: I'd want to be the one the robot calls when it doesn't know what to do.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Sara keeps her wedding, house and children plans intact. She wants to be the human the robot calls for help, which neatly sums up her steady approach. Staying in her fiancé's village is not up for debate.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it hits right after the wedding, and Daniel and I would both lose our trades. What would help is the farms training their own people on the new machines, paid, like an apprenticeship, and family close by.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about faith. People think farming's just a job, but for a lot of us it's tied to church and family and the village. If the work goes, I worry the rest goes with it.

headlineQuote: The robots can have the mud, I'll keep the night shifts with the sows.
portrait: Sara Silva is a 27-year-old who runs the farrowing paddocks on a 400-sow outdoor pig and grain farm. She's engaged to Daniel, a joiner, with a church wedding planned for next August and about two weeks of savings outside the wedding fund. Traditional and church-going, she blames supermarkets and paperwork and prefers apprenticeships to handouts. She uses AI now and then and learns new tools once proven. She's calm at a plateau and uneasy at steady change; AGI in two years alarms her and would shrink the wedding. With more warning her plans for a wedding, house and children survive, and she hopes to be the person a robot calls when a sow is in trouble.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it would hit right after the wedding and both she and her fiancé would lose their trades.
whatWouldHelp: Farms paying to train their own workers on the new machines, like an apprenticeship, with family nearby for support.
